ground_truth: Yes. If changes are intended to become part of the shipped public spec, they should be merged to public/main. Spec owners are responsible for porting specs between main and any other branches they use. private/main is for pre-review of changes that are not yet ready for the public repo, not the final shipped location. Once a spec version is merged to public/main, it is considered shipped and that API version should not be changed further. Custom team branches are owner-managed rather than specially supported platform branches, so they can be used for ongoing development, but shipping a version means moving it to public/main. testcase: Which repo is the source of truth and who must sync spec changes?

title: Which repo is the source of truth and who must sync spec changes?

question: In the Azure API specs workflow, which branch or repo is treated as the source of truth for public specs, what is private/RPSaaSMaster for, and who is responsible for keeping service-owned spec content synchronized between public/main, private/RPSaaSMaster, and any external source repo such as ADO? Why has this become more noticeable with TypeSpec?
ground_truth:
For public specifications, public/main is treated as the source of truth. Private/RPSaaSMaster is a staging branch used by RPaaS specs, not the authoritative source for public content. Service owners are responsible for synchronizing their service-owned spec files between public/main, private/RPSaaSMaster, and any external repository such as ADO; that synchronization is not handled automatically for RP-owned content.

The branch flow itself was not described as having fundamentally changed. What became more visible with TypeSpec is that other contributors may now make useful edits directly to a service's spec files more often than before. Earlier, once swagger was merged to public/main, it was much less common for others to edit the spec itself. That makes the existing sync responsibility more noticeable and creates friction for teams whose operational source remains outside the specs repo.

When introducing a new preview API version after an older preview in azure-rest-api-specs, how should PRs be structured so repository validation tooling handles the change correctly?
ground_truth:
Before interpreting other validation results, get TypeSpec validation passing so the generated TypeSpec output, swagger, and examples are in sync.

For repository workflow, avoid bundling changes to multiple swagger API versions in one PR. The validation tooling works best when a PR adds, removes, or changes only one swagger API version at a time. When introducing a new preview after a previous preview, remove the older preview from the TypeSpec source so the current TypeSpec models only the new preview, but leave the previously generated old preview swagger files in the repository unchanged. The PR for the new preview therefore should not modify the old preview swagger.

If the old preview swagger needs to be deleted, do that in a separate PR. Combining deletion of the old preview swagger with addition of the new preview swagger in the same PR can run into tooling limitations around delete/add or rename handling and can confuse breaking-change evaluation.

title: When to use a protected release-* branch versus a normal branch

question: In azure-rest-api-specs, when should teams use a protected release-* branch versus a normal branch for multi-team feature integration, and what are the tradeoffs?
ground_truth: Using a release branch is optional and involves tradeoffs. Any branch can be used for individual or team development, and pull requests to main or RPSaaSMaster can come from either a release branch or a non-release branch. The special behavior comes from the branch name pattern: if a branch is named release-*, it is treated as a protected branch, so pull requests into it must satisfy required protections such as passing required checks and approvals like ARMSignedOff. These branches are useful when teams want incremental ARM reviews during development or want a shared branch where changes are merged only after meeting quality gates. A branch with any other name is a normal branch without those protections, so teams can push directly, merge from main directly, and use it more freely. Use a normal branch when flexibility is more important; use a release-* branch when enforced checks and approvals on the shared integration branch are the goal.
